The reproductive biology of Rana chensinensis has been documented primarily through field observations in northeastern China. Females deposit their eggs in a single annual clutch, with reported clutch sizes ranging from 800 to 1500 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 800 to 1500 eggs per clutch], and typically only one clutch is laid each year [F_R_i = one clutch is laid each year], at a maintained temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The eggs themselves are roughly 3 millimeters in diameter, and upon hatching after an embryonic period of 50 days [ab = 50 days] at 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the newly emerged larvae possess a minimal wet weight of just 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams]. This extraordinarily low initial mass, among the lowest recorded for temperate ranid frogs, reflects the yolk-dependent, endotrophic phase of early development, wherein the tadpole relies entirely on internal reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The larval period involves filter feeding on algae and detritus, during which the tadpole grows rapidly within the constraints of its aquatic environment.

As the aquatic tadpole progresses through Gosner stages, a key developmental milestone is metamorphosis, which is marked by a complete body plan reorganisation. At the point of metamorphic climax, when tail resorption and limb development are largely complete, individuals measure approximately 1.4 centimeters  in snout-vent length. This length at metamorphosis represents the culmination of the larval growth phase and the start of a more terrestrial juvenile existence. Following this transformation, the recently metamorphosed froglets, or metamorphlings, embark on a period of rapid somatic growth. The juvenile stage is characterized by a shift in diet from filter feeding to active insectivory, allowing for the accumulation of body mass needed to reach reproductive maturity. Field surveys have indicated that the snout-vent length at which female frogs attain puberty is around 5.0 centimeters [Lp = around 5.0 centimeters], a size that is achieved after a considerable period of post-metamorphic feeding and growth.

Sexual maturation in Rana chensinensis is closely tied to thermal conditions encountered in its temperate habitat. Under field conditions reflective of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at which females reach sexual maturity is approximately 730 days [tp = approximately 730 days]. This two-year developmental delay is typical for ranid frogs inhabiting seasonal environments, where a full growing season is often required to accumulate sufficient energy reserves before the first overwintering period. Once attained, the size at puberty for females is biologically meaningful; the 5.0 centimeters [Lp = 5.0 centimeters] snout-vent length represents a threshold that allows for the physical accommodation and mobilization of resources for the development of a substantial clutch of eggs. Interestingly, the timing of this maturation is not fixed and can vary with local thermal regimes, but the available data converge on this approximate two-year interval for populations experiencing typical seasonal temperature cycles in the northern part of the species' range.

Considerable sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size is evident upon reaching full adult growth. Adult female frogs achieve a maximum snout-vent length of 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters], which corresponds to a maximum wet body weight of 20.2 grams [Wwi = 20.2 grams] in gravid individuals. This ultimate wet weight is substantially greater than that of males, reflecting the high energetic investment females must make in oocyte production and the physical space required for a developing clutch. Males, in contrast, reach a smaller final size, with an ultimate snout-vent length of only 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters], a difference that is likely driven by sexual selection for male mobility and territorial behavior rather than for fecundity. This pattern of female-biased size dimorphism is common among anurans where female fecundity scales positively with body volume. The mass of an adult female, for instance, scales isometrically with the cube of length, explaining the pronounced divergence in body mass despite a relatively modest difference in linear dimensions between the sexes.

Maximum longevity in wild populations of Rana chensinensis is estimated to be around 6 years [am = around 6 years] under natural thermal conditions at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This lifespan is comparatively modest for a frog of this body size, though it is consistent with the high predation pressure and seasonal mortality typical of temperate amphibian communities. The oldest documented individuals are typically those that survive multiple breeding seasons, with reproductive senescence likely setting in after the fourth or fifth year. Throughout their adult lives, females annually produce a single clutch of eggs [F_R_i = annually produce a single clutch of eggs], each containing between 800 and 1500 eggs [N_R_i = each containing between 800 and 1500 eggs], a strategy that buffers against the high variability in juvenile survival that characterizes ephemeral breeding ponds. The combination of a modest lifespan, delayed maturity, and low annual fecundity places this species firmly on the slower end of the amphibian life-history continuum.
